verses.zh: 第九年十月初十日，耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month:[NOTE:1]
notes: The date of this oracle was January 15, 588 b.c.

verses.zh: 「人子啊，今日正是巴比伦王就近耶路撒冷的日子，你要将这日记下，
verses.en: “Son of man, write down the name of this day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege[NOTE:1] to Jerusalem[NOTE:2] this very day.
notes: Heb “lean on, put pressure on.”
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

verses.zh: 要向这悖逆之家设比喻说，主耶和华如此说：将锅放在火上，放好了，就倒水在其中；
verses.en: Recite a proverb to this rebellious house[NOTE:1] and say to them, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord says:“‘Set on the pot,[NOTE:2] set it on, pour water in it too;
notes: The book of Ezekiel frequently refers to the Israelites as a rebellious house (Ezek 2:5, 6, 8; 3:9, 26-27; 12:2-3, 9, 25; 17:12; 24:3).
See Ezek 11:3-12.

verses.zh: 将肉块，就是一切肥美的肉块、腿，和肩都聚在其中，拿美好的骨头把锅装满；
verses.en: add the pieces of meat to it, every good piece,the thigh and the shoulder;fill it with choice bones.

verses.zh: 取羊群中最好的，将柴堆在锅下，使锅开滚，好把骨头煮在其中。
verses.en: Take the choice bone of the flock,heap up wood under it;boil rapidly,and boil its bones in it.

verses.zh: 「主耶和华如此说：祸哉！这流人血的城，就是长锈的锅。其中的锈未曾除掉，须要将肉块从其中一一取出来，不必为它拈阄。
verses.en: “‘Therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says:Woe to the city of bloodshed,the pot whose rot[NOTE:1] is in it,whose rot has not been removed[NOTE:2] from it!Empty it piece by piece.No lot has fallen on it.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “rust.”
Heb “has not gone out.”
Here “lot” may refer to the decision made by casting lots; it is not chosen at all.

verses.zh: 城中所流的血倒在净光的磐石上，不倒在地上，用土掩盖。
verses.en: For her blood was in it;she poured it on an exposed rock;she did not pour it on the ground to cover it up with dust.

verses.zh: 这城中所流的血倒在净光的磐石上，不得掩盖，乃是出于我，为要发忿怒施行报应。
verses.en: To arouse anger, to take vengeance,I have placed her blood on an exposed rock so that it cannot be covered up.

verses.zh: 所以主耶和华如此说：祸哉！这流人血的城，我也必大堆火柴，
verses.en: “‘Therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says: Woe to the city of bloodshed!I will also make the pile high.

verses.zh: 添上木柴，使火着旺，将肉煮烂，把汤熬浓，使骨头烤焦；
verses.en: Pile up the wood, kindle the fire;cook the meat well, mix in the spices,and let the bones be charred.

verses.zh: 把锅倒空坐在炭火上，使锅烧热，使铜烧红，熔化其中的污秽，除净其上的锈。
verses.en: Set the empty pot on the coals,[NOTE:1] until it becomes hot and its copper glows,until its uncleanness melts within it and its rot[NOTE:2] is consumed.
notes: Heb “set it upon its coals, empty.”
Or “rust” (so also in v. 12).

verses.zh: 这锅劳碌疲乏，所长的大锈仍未除掉；这锈就是用火也不能除掉。
verses.en: It has tried my patience;[NOTE:1] yet its thick rot is not removed[NOTE:2] from it.Subject its rot to the fire![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “(with) toil she has wearied.” The meaning of the statement is unclear in the Hebrew text; some follow the LXX and delete it. The first word in the statement (rendered “toil” in the literal translation above) occurs only here in the OT, and the verb “she has wearied” lacks a stated object. Elsewhere the Hiphil of the verb refers to wearying someone or trying someone’s patience. The feminine subject is apparently the symbolic pot.
Heb “does not go out.”
Heb “in fire its rust.” The meaning of the expression is unclear. The translation understands the statement as a command to burn the rust away. See D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:768.

verses.zh: 在你污秽中有淫行，我洁净你，你却不洁净。你的污秽再不能洁净，直等我向你发的忿怒止息。
verses.en: You mix uncleanness with obscene conduct.[NOTE:1] I tried to cleanse you,[NOTE:2] but you are not clean.You will not be cleansed from your uncleanness[NOTE:3] until I have exhausted my anger on you.
notes: Heb “in your uncleanness (is) obscene conduct.”

Heb “because I cleansed you.” In this context (see especially the very next statement), the statement must refer to divine intention and purpose. Despite God’s efforts to cleanse his people, they resisted him and remained morally impure.
The Hebrew text adds the word “again.”

verses.zh: 我―耶和华说过的必定成就，必照话而行，必不返回，必不顾惜，也不后悔。人必照你的举动行为审判你。这是主耶和华说的。」
verses.en: “‘I, the Lord, have spoken; judgment[NOTE:1] is coming and I will act! I will not relent, or show pity, or be sorry![NOTE:2] I will judge you[NOTE:3] according to your conduct[NOTE:4] and your deeds, declares the Sovereign Lord.’”
notes: Heb “it”; the referent has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or perhaps, “change my mind.”

Some medieval Hebrew mss and the major ancient versions read a first person verb here. Most Hebrew mss read have an indefinite subject, “they will judge you,” which could be translated, “you will be judged.”
Heb “ways.”

verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 「人子啊，我要将你眼目所喜爱的忽然取去，你却不可悲哀哭泣，也不可流泪，
verses.en: “Son of man, realize that I am about to take the delight of your eyes away from you with a jolt,[NOTE:1] but you must not mourn or weep or shed tears.
notes: Heb “a strike.”

verses.zh: 只可叹息，不可出声，不可办理丧事；头上仍勒裹头巾，脚上仍穿鞋，不可蒙着嘴唇，也不可吃吊丧的食物。」
verses.en: Groan to moan for the dead,[NOTE:1] but do not perform mourning rites.[NOTE:2] Bind on your turban[NOTE:3] and put your sandals on your feet. Do not cover your lip[NOTE:4] and do not eat food brought by others.”[NOTE:5]
notes: As it stands in the MT, the syntax is difficult. Most translations say something like “groan in silence,” but this is problematic. According to their form, the two verbs that begin the verse, הֵאָנֵק (heʾanek; to groan) and דֹּם (dom; to be silent), may each be parsed as either imperative or infinitive construct. This allows four possible sequences. An infinitive followed by an infinitive would lack a main verb and can be dismissed. An infinitive followed by an imperative is improper syntax and nowhere occurs with both in the same clause. An imperative followed by an infinitive is very rare. The only three clear cases (Ps 33:3; Isa 1:16; 23:16) appear to involve infinitive complements, which does not fit these terms. Two imperatives back to back are common, occurring over 200 times, but in no case does the second imperative tell the manner of the action in the first (except perhaps a couple disputable parsings of מַהֵר (maher; be quick). So there is no combination of the forms in the MT that supports the common translation. It may also be said that groaning and being silent are mutually exclusive concepts. However, there is a rare homonym, also attested in the cognate languages Ugaritic and Akkadian, another root דמם (dmm), which means to moan. The translation above follows the suggestion of M. Greenberg that דֹּם מֵתִים (dom metim) be taken together and דֹּם be derived from דָּמַם (damam, “to moan, murmur”) meaning: “Groan a moaning for the dead.” See M. Greenberg, Ezekiel (AB), 2:508. Note that in verse 23 Ezekiel affirms that the people will moan to each other (though there the root is נָהַם, naham); therefore, it is reasonable to suppose that Ezekiel is moaning here, since his actions forecast theirs.

Heb “(For) the dead mourning you shall not conduct.” In the Hebrew text the word translated “dead” is plural, indicating that mourning rites are in view. Such rites would involve outward demonstrations of one’s sorrow, including wailing and weeping.
The turban would normally be removed for mourning (Josh 7:6; 1 Sam 4:12).
Mourning rites included covering the lower part of the face. See Lev 13:45.

Heb “the bread of men.” The translation follows the suggestion accepted by M. Greenberg (Ezekiel [AB], 2:509) that this refers to a meal brought by comforters to the one mourning. Some repoint the consonantal text to read “the bread of despair” (see L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 2:56), while others, with support from the Targum and Vulgate, emend the consonantal text to read “the bread of mourners” (see D. I. Block, Ezekiel [NICOT], 1:784).

verses.zh: 于是我将这事早晨告诉百姓，晚上我的妻就死了。次日早晨我便遵命而行。
verses.en: So I spoke to the people in the morning, and my wife died in the evening. In the morning[NOTE:1] I acted just as I was commanded.
notes: This almost certainly refers to the following morning. For a discussion of various interpretive options in understanding the chronology reflected in verse 18, see D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:790.

verses.zh: 百姓问我说：「你这样行与我们有甚么关系，你不告诉我们么？」
verses.en: Then the people said to me, “Will you not tell us what these things you are doing mean for us?”

verses.zh: 我回答他们：「耶和华的话临到我说：
verses.en: So I said to them: “The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 『你告诉以色列家，主耶和华如此说：我必使我的圣所，就是你们势力所夸耀、眼里所喜爱、心中所爱惜的被亵渎，并且你们所遗留的儿女必倒在刀下。
verses.en: Say to the house of Israel, ‘This is what the Sovereign Lord says: Realize I am about to desecrate my sanctuary—the source of your confident pride,[NOTE:1] the object in which your eyes delight,[NOTE:2] and your life’s passion.[NOTE:3] Your very own sons and daughters whom you have left behind will die[NOTE:4] by the sword.
notes: Heb “the pride of your strength” means “your strong pride.”

Heb “the delight of your eyes.” Just as Ezekiel was deprived of his beloved wife (v. 16, the “desire” of his “eyes”), so the Lord would be forced to remove the object of his devotion, the temple, which symbolized his close relationship to his covenant people.

Heb “the object of compassion of your soul.” The accentuation in the traditional Hebrew text indicates that the descriptive phrases (“the source of your confident pride, the object in which your eyes delight, and your life’s passion”) modify the preceding “my sanctuary.”
Heb “fall.”

verses.zh: 那时，你们必行我仆人所行的，不蒙着嘴唇，也不吃吊丧的食物。
verses.en: Then you will do as I have done: You will not cover your lip or eat food brought by others.[NOTE:1]
notes: See v. 17.

verses.zh: 你们仍要头上勒裹头巾，脚上穿鞋；不可悲哀哭泣。你们必因自己的罪孽相对叹息，渐渐消灭。
verses.en: Your turbans will be on your heads and your sandals on your feet; you will not mourn or weep, but you will rot[NOTE:1] for your iniquities[NOTE:2] and groan among yourselves.
notes: The same verb appears in 4:17 and 33:10.

Or “in your punishment.” The phrase “in/for [a person’s] iniquity/punishment” occurs fourteen times in Ezekiel: here; 3:18, 19; 4:17; 7:13, 16; 18:17, 18, 19, 20; 33:6, 8, 9; 39:23. The Hebrew word for “iniquity” may also mean the “punishment” for iniquity or “guilt” of iniquity.

verses.zh: 以西结必这样为你们作预兆；凡他所行的，你们也必照样行。那事来到，你们就知道我是主耶和华。
verses.en: Ezekiel will be an object lesson for you; you will do all that he has done. When it happens, then you will know that I am the Sovereign Lord.’

verses.zh: 「人子啊，我除掉他们所倚靠、所欢喜的荣耀，并眼中所喜爱、心里所重看的儿女。
verses.en: “And you, son of man, this is what will happen on the day I take[NOTE:1] from them their stronghold—their beautiful source of joy, the object in which their eyes delight, and the main concern of their lives,[NOTE:2] as well as their sons and daughters:[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “(Will) it not (be) in the day I take?”

Heb “the uplifting of their soul.” According to BDB 672 s.v. מַשָּׂא 2, the term “uplifting” refers to “that to which they lift up their soul, their heart’s desire.” However, this text is the only one listed for this use. It seems more likely here that the term has its well-attested nuance of “burden, load,” referring to that which weighs them down emotionally and is a constant source of concern or worry.

In the Hebrew text there is no conjunction before “their sons and daughters.” For this reason one might assume that the preceding descriptive phrases refer to the sons and daughters, but verse 21 suggests otherwise. The descriptive phrases appear to refer to the “stronghold,” which parallels “my sanctuary” in verse 21. The children constitute a separate category.

verses.zh: 那日逃脱的人岂不来到你这里，使你耳闻这事吗？
verses.en: On that day a fugitive will come to you to report the news.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “to make the ears hear.”

verses.zh: 你必向逃脱的人开口说话，不再哑口。你必这样为他们作预兆，他们就知道我是耶和华。」
verses.en: On that day you will be able to speak again;[NOTE:1] you will talk with the fugitive and be silent no longer. You will be an object lesson for them, and they will know that I am the Lord.”
notes: Heb “your mouth will open.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the four modern translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

- First paragraph

- Second paragraph

- Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 24:1-5

1And the word of the Lord came to me in the ninth year, in the tenth month,
on the tenth of the month, saying, 2"Son of man, write the name of the day, this very day. The king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day.
3Speak a parable to the rebellious house and say to them, 'Thus says the Lord God,

"Put on the pot, put it on and also pour water in it;

4 Put in it the pieces,

Every good piece, the thigh and the shoulder;

Fill it with choice bones.

5Take the choicest of the flock,

And also pile wood under the pot.

Make it boil vigorously.

Also seethe its bones in it."

24:1 This is the fourth date (cf. Ezek. 1:2; 8:1; 20:1) listed in Ezekiel. Surprisingly one would expect another date at chapter 25,
which starts the judgment context on the nations. This may mean chapters 24 and 25 are a literary unit.

This dates the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem (cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 39:1; 52:4). It was begun on January 15, 588
B.C. (NET Bible). The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 710, calculates the date as Jan. 5, 587 B.C.
It took until 586 B.C. for the city to fall. Remember, there are two ways to count the reign of kings in the ANE.

In a book of prophecy the question of final revision always comes into play. Did Ezekiel know the exact date of the siege
and later fall of Jerusalem? Of course he could; he was a prophet of YHWH. YHWH often used this predictive quality to encourage His people
that He was in control of history. However, it is also surely possible, without distracting from the power of YHWH or the foresight of His prophets,
to see these dates as literary. These books were, at some point, the collected and arranged prophecies of Ezekiel. Literary design does not diminish prophetic predictions!

Special Topic: Inspiration

Special Topic: The Bible (its uniqueness and inspiration)

24:2 "Son of man" See note at Ezek. 2:1.

▣ "write" The MT has "write" (BDB 507, KB 503) as a Qal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE ,
but the Masoretic scholars suggested it be read (Qere) as a Qal IMPERATIVE
(same kind of problem as in Ezek. 24:10).

There are many IMPERATIVES in this chapter (cf. Ezek. 24:2,3 [three], 4,5 [two], 6,10 [two], 11,17[two],
21. Most of them occur in the poetic section (i.e. Ezek. 24:3b-5, 6-13) and are directed to the rebellious house (i.e. Judah).

Special Topic: Masoretic Text

▣ "the name of the day, this very day" Judgment on Jerusalem was not a future prediction, but a terrible reality (i.e. Lev. 26; Deut. 28)!

▣ "has laid siege" The VERB (BDB 701, KB 759, Qal PERFECT) is literally
"lean on," but is used here as an idiom of a city being besieged (Jerusalem's siege is begun, cf. 2 Kgs. 25:1; Jer. 39:1; 52:4).

24:3-5 This first poetic stanza has several commands from YHWH which set the stage for the parable/proverb.

- put on the pot, BDB 1046, KB 1636, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3

- put it on, BDB 1046, KB 1636, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3

- pour, BDB 427, KB 428, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:3

- put (lit. gather), BDB 62, KB 74, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:4

- fill, BDB 569, KB 583, Piel IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:4

- pile, BDB 189, KB 217, Qal IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:5

- boil, BDB 958, KB 1299, Piel IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:5

24:3 "speak a parable" This (BDB 605, KB 647) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. See
note at Ezek. 12:22,23; 17:2; 18:2, 3; 20:49. Ezekiel used several poems to communicate YHWH's messages.

- poem of Judah as a ruined vine, Ezek. 19

- poem of the sharp, bright, swift sword of judgment, Ezek. 21:9-10

- poem of the large cup of drunkenness, Ezek. 23:32-34

- poem of the corrupted, large, bronze (cf. Ezek. 24:11) cooking pot, Ezek. 24:3-13

- poems about the fall of Tyre, Ezek. 26:17-18; 27:3-9,25-36; 28:2-19

- poems about the fall of Egypt, Ezek. 29:3-7; 30:2-19; 31:2-9; 32:2-8,12-15

▣ "to the rebellious house" This (BDB 598, cf. Ezek. 2:5,6,8; 3:9,26,27; 12:2[twice],3,9,25; 17:12;
Isa. 30:9) is a derogatory way of referring to faithless Judah (cf. Ezek. 2:6,8).

The idiom is repeated with the PARTICIPLE of the
VERB (BDB 597, KB 632) in Ezek. 2:3 (also note the use of the parallel terms

- BDB 833, KB 981 in Isa. 1:2

- BDB 710 in Isa. 30:1

Judah's stubborn rebellion (cf. Deut. 9:5-6,13; 10:16; 31:27) has been continual and purposeful! I think
YHWH chose Israel with all her weaknesses to clearly reveal His faithfulness in the stark light of their unfaithfulness! If YHWH
can continue to love, forgive, and use Israel, then there is a great hope for all of Adam's children, based solely on the unchanging,
merciful, gracious character of YHWH!

Special Topic: Stubbornness

Special Topic: Characteristics of Israel's God

Special Topic: YHWH's Eternal Redemptive Plan

▣ This chapter is based on Jeremiah's parable about a boiling pot (cf. Jer. 1:13, 14).

24:4-5 The very best pieces of the very best of the flock were put in the pot. Who does this refer to?

- the royal, priestly, and civic leaders who remained in Jerusalem, cf. Jer. 39:6; 52:10,24-27

- national Israel herself when YHWH found her in the wilderness, Ezek. 16:4-14

In this context of the citizens of Jerusalem seeing themselves as the "lucky ones," "spared ones,"
"better ones" than those taken into exile, this phrase may well refer to all of them! However, they will be
destroyed and YHWH will choose to work with and restore the early exiles! This was shocking to the arrogant, sinful
Judeans still in Jerusalem and Judah.

24:5

NASB, TEV, NJB, REB
"wood"

NKJV
"fuel bones"

LXX, Peshitta
"bones"

JPSOA
"the cuts"

The MT has "bones" (BDB 782, v. 4), but "wood" or "logs" (BDB 781, v. 10) fits the context better.

- the bones ‒ העצמים

- the logs ‒ העצים

However, the UBS Text Project, p. 78, thinks "bones" (BDB782) is original (an "A" rating). "Bones" appears again at the end of v. 5.

▣ "Make it boil vigorously" This is the VERB (BDB 958, KB 1299, Piel IMPERATIVE) and
the NOUN of the same root for intensity (i.e. "vigorously").

This is paralleled with "seethe" (BDB 143, KB 164, Qal PERFECT). The cooking is imagery for YHWH's complete judgment.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 24:6-14

6Therefore, thus says the Lord God,

"Woe to the bloody city,

To the pot in which there is rust

And whose rust has not gone out of it!

Take out of it piece after piece,

Without making a choice.

7For her blood is in her midst;

She placed it on the bare rock;

She did not pour it on the ground

To cover it with dust.

8That it may cause wrath to come up to take vengeance,

I have put her blood on the bare rock,

That it may not be covered."

9Therefore, thus says the Lord God,

"Woe to the bloody city!

I also will make the pile great.

10Heap on the wood, kindle the fire,

Boil the flesh well

And mix in the spices,

And let the bones be burned.

11Then set it empty on its coals

So that it may be hot

And its bronze may glow

And its filthiness may be melted in it,

Its rust consumed.

12She has wearied Me with toil,

Yet her great rust has not gone from her;

Let her rust be in the fire!

13In your filthiness is lewdness.

Because I would have cleansed you,

Yet you are not clean,

You will not be cleansed from your filthiness again

Until I have spent My wrath on you.

14I, the Lord, have spoken; it is coming and I will act. I will
not relent, and I will not pity and I will not be sorry; according to your ways and according to your deeds I will judge you," declares the Lord God.'"

24:6 "Woe" This INTERJECTION (BDB 17, cf. Ezek. 24:9) expresses deep emotion often connected to judgment
(cf. Ezek. 16:23; Jer. 4:13; 6:4; 10:19; 13:27; 15:10; Hosea 7:13).

▣ "the bloody city" See note at Ezek. 22:2.

NASB, NRSV
"rust"

NKJV, JPSOA
"scum" (i.e. left at the bottom of the pit)

TEV
"corroded"

NJB
"rusty"

REB
"green with corrosion"

LXX
"blight," "rust," or "scum"

Peshitta
"is set on the fire" (from v. 5)

This Hebrew word is uncertain ((BDB 316, KB 315). It is found only in this chapter in the OT.
The same trilateral root means "rust" in Arabic. YHWH had tried to cleanse His people over and over again, but
their sin was too deep (i.e. Genesis 3; see Special Topic: The Fall of Mankind).

▣ "Without making a choice" This VERB (lit. "fall," BDB 656,
KB 709, Qal PERFECT) was used of casting lots to know YHWH's will.

- dividing the Promised Land among the tribes, Num. 34:2; Josh. 13:6; 23:4; Ezek. 45:1

- dividing the duties in the temple, 1 Chr. 24:31; 26:13,14

- determining who would supply wood for the new sacrificial system, Neh. 10:34

- determining who would live in the rebuilt Jerusalem, Neh. 11:1

- determining the guilty party, Jonah 1:7

This phrase seems to imply that death would come indiscriminately to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

24:7 This refers to the openness and flagrant nature (i.e. "places it on a bare rock," i.e. in the sight of
all) of Judah's sin. This refers to:

- an allusion to a priestly act of draining the blood from sacrificial animals and putting it on the appropriate
places (Leviticus 1-7). The remainder was poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifice (see Special Topic: Altar of Sacrifice)

- the proper slaughter of wild animals to be consumed (cf. Lev. 17:13; Deut. 12:16; see Special Topic: Food Laws).

▣ "To cover it with dust" This seems to refer to the blood of their victims (cf. Lev. 17:13).

24:8 As Judah flagrantly sinned for all to see, now YHWH will judge her for all to see (cf. Deut. 29:24-28;
Jer. 16:10; 22:8,9).

24:9-10 This is a reflection of Ezek. 24:3b-5. The pot of judgment is boiling and Judah is in it!

Verses 10-11 have a series of commands related to the boiling pot.

- heap, BDB 915, KB 1176, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 24:5b, 9c

- kindle, BDB 196, KB 223, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ezek. 24:5c

- boil, BDB 1070, KB 1752, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- (John J. Owens, Analytical Keys to the Old Testament, vol. 4, p. 572, calls it
a Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- Beall, Banks, Smith, Old Testament Parsing Guide, p. 619, calls it
a Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE

- Benjamin Davidson, Analytical Hebrew and Chaldee Lexicon of the Old Testament, p. 231,
gives both options).

- mix, BDB 955, KB 1289, Hiphil IMPERATIVE (Owens)
or INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE (Beall, Banks, Smith) or either (Davidson)

- set, BDB 763, KB 840, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, Ezek. 24:11

24:11 The empty pot (cf. Ezek. 24:11) is set on the hot coals and the remaining scum (or "rust, v. 6")

24:12 "She has wearied Me with toil" This refers to YHWH's attempt to bring Judah to repentance.
He made a great and continuous effort to bring her back to Himself. This phrase is difficult to understand
because

- the MASCULINE PLURAL NOUN "toil" (BDB 20) is unusual and found only
here in the OT

- the VERB has no OBJECT

- the LXX omits it

therefore, some scholars see it as an addition.

Notice how the JPSOA translates these three poetic lines:

"It has frustrated all efforts,

Its thick scum will not leave it‒

Into the fire with its scum!"

The "it" would refer to the copper cooking pot.

24:13 "lewdness" This term (BDB 273) describes Judah's idolatry, of which they refuse to give up and respond appropriately

BDB 628, KB 679, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) denotes that at some point

He will judge Judah according to her ways and deeds (cf. Ezek. 7:3,8,27; 18:30; 36:19). This is figurative language for

24:16-17 "the desire of your eyes" This shows the tenderness of Ezekiel toward his wife. This also is the imagery used in
verses 16-24 to describe the unbelievable pain of the people of Judah when Jerusalem fell.

In Ezekiel's pain he is told to

- not mourn, BDB 704, KB 763, Qal IMPERFECT, negated

- not weep, BDB 113, KB 129, Qal IMPERFECT, negated

- no tears shall run down, BDB 97, KB 112, Qal IMPERFECT, negated,
because this phrase

- is left out of the LXX

- does not fit the parallelism

- is redundant with #2, many scholars think it is an addition

This is similar to YHWH's message about grieving to Jeremiah (cf. Jer. 16:5).

Just a personal note, it is always hard for me, being a modern western person, to not be affected
as an interpreter by my culture's overemphasis on the rights and value of the individual. Most societies in
the world are tribal or clan-focused. It bothers me when

- Job's children die

- David's child dies

- Jeremiah is told not to marry

- YHWH takes Ezekiel's wife

My mind screams to me "Are not these affected individuals as important to God as the biblical
characters? Does not God love and care for them? Do not His promises cover them?" Do you hear the twenty-first
century American in me?

God has a universal plan. This world is affected by sin. This life is only the beginning of an
eternal relationship! Yes, God loves and cares for individuals, but He has bigger and better plans for all humanity.
This is not the world God intended it to be!

Theologically I know that the OT attributes all causality to God as a way of affirming monotheism!
He, and only He, is in control. Individuals get hurt, die, both by natural causes and by the hand of evil,
manipulative people. Yet God's promises are still sure! He does care for each, but also for all (cf. 2 Cor. 5:21)!
The book by Hannah Whithall Smith, The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life, has really helped me in
this area.

24:17 This is a series of Hebrew cultural images describing mourning rites (cf. Jer. 16:5-13). Ezekiel was
not allowed to mourn ("be silent," BDB 198, KB 266, Qal IMPERATIVE) for the
death of his own wife. The things he was expected to do, he was told to do the opposite.

- put on your hat

- put on your shoes

- do not cover your mouth

- do not eat mourner's bread

Ezekiel's grief (i.e. Ezek. 24:22) over the loss of his wife parallels YHWH's grief over the
loss of His wife (i.e. Judah). However, Judah's judgment was appropriate! Grieving over them would imply
that the judgment was not deserved, appropriate, and necessary (e.g. Lev. 10:1-7 in Nadab and Abihu's death).

24:21 Notice the parallel phrases YHWH uses to describe Judah's feelings toward the temple.

- the pride of your power

- the desire of your eyes

- the delight of your soul

Judah had substituted devotion to a building for their devotion to YHWH (e.g. Jer. 7). This is always a problem
for religiously oriented people! The goal is fellowship with God (cf. Ps. 42:1-2; 63:1; 143:6). It is an orientation of the heart, not a physical
place to worship, or human performance.

24:23 "you will rot away in your iniquities" This VERB (BDB 596, KB 628, Niphal PERFECT
with waw) is used several times by Ezekiel (cf. Ezek. 4:17; 33:10) and may reflect Lev. 26:39. Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's condemnations of
both Israel and Judah reflect the terminology of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. Remember, both of them were from priestly families.

24:24 Notice the direct speech of YHWH where Ezekiel is mentioned by name. The prophet himself is a sign
(cf. Ezek. 24:27; 12:11).

YHWH addresses Ezekiel directly in Ezek. 24:25-27. We, as later readers of the OT, know more about
the man Ezekiel from this chapter than from any other OT prophet. We sense his love for his wife and his people.
We feel his pain over Judean sin and incalcitrance!

25"'As for you, son of man, will it not be on the day when I take from them their stronghold,
the joy of their pride, the desire of their eyes and their heart's delight, their sons and their daughters, 26that on that day he who escapes will come to

24:25 Notice the list of things the Judeans trusted in and longed for.

- their stronghold (i.e. Jerusalem)

- the joy of their pride (i.e. the temple, see Jeremiah's temple sermon in Jer. 7)

- the desire of their eyes (i.e. the temple)

- their heart's delight (i.e. their idols)

- their children (i.e. exile or death)

See not at 24:21.

24:27 "On that day your mouth will be opened" Originally, after the vision of Ezekiel in chapter 1, God told the prophet that he would
be unable to speak at times (cf. Ezek. 3:26). Therefore, these opening chapters of Ezekiel deal quite often with symbolic action. However, after the
Fall of Jerusalem, the prophet's mouth was opened (cf. Ezek. 3:27; 33:22) and his message changed from doom/judgment to forgiveness/restoration!
Now he could preach hope, restoration, and the renewal of covenant promises.

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.
